$comment: THE SQLITE HARNESS LEG CATALOGUE — the declared, HOST-FREE answer to 'which targets does this harness build?'. D-HARNESS-CROSS-HOST-ANY-TARGET item (2). ★ THE RULE THIS FILE EXISTS TO ENFORCE: the set of legs is a property of the HARNESS, not of the machine running it. Read this file on Windows, on Linux, on an arm64 VPS or on a Mac and you get the SAME five legs. What the host changes is ONLY whether it can EXECUTE a leg's artifact — a separate question, answered by `runOn` + `launchers` below and never by an `if host == ...` in a driver. Before this file existed, build-and-test.sh derived its leg list from `uname` (pe64 was unreachable from any host, macho only from a Mac) and build-and-test.ps1 refused to start unless $IsWindows (pe64 was its ONLY leg, hardcoded). Each driver therefore conflated HOST with TARGET, which is the opposite of the user's hard requirement: 'build ANY target inside ANY host, this MUST work.'
$vocabularyComment: The declaration vocabulary is the CORPUS's, not a new one: `spec` and `runOn` mean exactly what they mean in examples/**/expected.json, and the verdicts a driver records for a leg come from the closed 7+1-name set in tests/test_support/arm_verdict_ledger.hpp (pinned by tests/harness/test_sqlite_harness_legs.cpp, which compares this catalogue's resolver output against that C++ enum). `launchers` is the ONE strict extension: the corpus's `emulator` key covers a cross-ARCH host on the SAME OS, and this harness additionally needs the cross-OS case (a pe64 artifact under Wine on Linux), so both are expressed as one ordered list of declared launchers keyed by (hostOs, hostArch). Absence of a matching launcher entry IS the 'none declared' declaration — there is no empty-string spelling, so a reader cannot mistake 'we looked and there is none' for 'nobody filled this in'. ★ EVERY launcher entry additionally declares `pathTranslation`: the PATH NAMESPACE its argv lives in, from the closed set in harness_legs.py (`none`, `windows-to-wsl`). It is required on every entry, never defaulted, for the same reason `zconfGuards` is: a reader must not have to know a default, and `none` — 'this launcher takes the driver's paths verbatim' — is a CLAIM about the launcher, not an absence. It exists because a launcher need not share a filesystem namespace with the driver that spawns it: `wine /home/me/x.exe` takes the driver's own path, `wsl.exe` needs `/mnt/c/...` where the driver holds a drive-letter path, and an untranslated path does not fail as a path error — the callee opens a relative file by that name, misses, and the run reads as a broken binary. The verb is resolved and APPLIED by harness_legs.py (`--translate-path` / `--assert-translated`), so the translator is named in one file and not in two drivers. ★★ AND `envTransfer`, THE SECOND HALF OF THE SAME FACT, found by measuring the first: a launcher in another OS namespace does not inherit the driver's ENVIRONMENT either. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-04 — a `wsl.exe`-launched fixture saw `SQLITE_TEST_PATTERN_LIST` and `QUICKTEST_OMIT` as EMPTY, so the corpus RESUME ENGINE (which selects its files through that variable) silently re-ran the corpus from the beginning instead of from the abort point: a harness that looks like it is working and is not. `inherit` = the child gets this driver's environment block (qemu, Wine, `arch`); `wslenv` = each variable must be NAMED in the `WSLENV` carrier. Resolved by harness_legs.py (`--env-transfer`), so the carrier and its separator are spelled once.
$noHostKeyingComment: NOTHING in this file may be keyed on the host. `build.libraries.searchPaths` is the one place host-shaped STRINGS appear, and they are CANDIDATES, not decisions: every path is tried on every host, a hit is used and a miss costs nothing. A driver that skips a search path because of the host it is on has reintroduced the defect. ⚠ If you are tempted to add a `"onlyOnHost"` key here, stop: the question you are answering is either 'can this host EXECUTE it' (that is `runOn`/`launchers`) or 'is a declared build input present' (that is a filesystem probe whose failure is the LOUD `skipped-build-input-missing` verdict) — never 'is this leg allowed to exist'.
$stagedHeadersComment: ★ THE THIRD-PARTY HEADERS A LEG COMPILES AGAINST ARE A TARGET FACT, NOT A HOST ONE (D-HARNESS-SQLITE-STAGE-ZCONF-IS-PE-SHAPED, closed TF-C115). The staged zlib header is copied from the DERIVING POSIX host, where `./configure` baked ITS OWN probe results into zconf.h — `#if 1 → #define Z_HAVE_UNISTD_H` and friends. Those are facts about the deriving machine, exactly like the recipe's HAVE_*/Z_HAVE_* defines that `recipeTransform` exists to drop, and handing them to a foreign target is the same cross-compile category error one level down. Each leg therefore DECLARES `build.zconfGuards` — the value ITS target has for each guard `./configure` may have set — and the drivers stage ONE zinc/ PER `recipeTransform` (stage-zinc.py, called by both) and give each leg an include list pointing at its own. Two legs may share a zinc/ only by sharing a recipeTransform, and the lint refuses a catalogue where same-transform legs declare different guards. Before this, ONE pe-shaped zinc/ served every leg and the .ps1 REFUSED (`poisoned`) any leg that was not `windows-selfconfig` rather than compile it against the wrong header — the right call, and the reason this key exists is to make the refusal unnecessary instead of relaxing it.

legs.label: elf64-x86_64
legs.$launchersComment: qemu-x86_64 lets an arm64 Linux host run this leg. ★ NOTE THE ASYMMETRY WITH THE CORPUS, which is a finding and not a copy error: examples/**/expected.json declares NO emulator on its (x86_64, linux) arms, so on the native arm64 Linux VPS every one of them is a structural skip even though qemu-x86_64 exists. This catalogue declares it; the corpus's omission is tracked separately (D-TEST-CORPUS-NO-QEMU-X86_64-ON-ARM64-HOST). ★★ `wsl.exe` IS THE SECOND ENTRY AND IT CLOSES D-HARNESS-NO-WSL-LAUNCHER-FOR-ELF-ON-WINDOWS. A Windows host BUILDS this leg (TF-C115 did) and could always have RUN it — the artefact built by build-and-test.ps1 passed 330,436 tests under WSL BY HAND — but nothing declared the launcher, so the driver recorded `skipped-by-runOn` beside a binary it had just produced. It is not a plain command entry: wsl.exe lives in a DIFFERENT PATH NAMESPACE from the driver that spawns it (`pathTranslation`) AND in a different ENVIRONMENT namespace (`envTransfer`). The second was found by measuring the first — with paths translated but the environment assumed to inherit, the corpus resume engine's file selection arrived EMPTY and the resume re-ran the whole corpus while looking like it worked.

build.$zconfGuardsComment: See the pe64 leg for the whole story. This target HAS <unistd.h>, so zlib must see it — which is what the deriving Linux host's ./configure already decided, so these values are the staged header's own.

legs.label: elf64-arm64
legs.$launchersComment: qemu-aarch64 for a cross-ARCH Linux host, and `wsl.exe` for the cross-OS case — the same pair, one arch over. ⚠ THE wsl.exe ENTRY IS DECLARED AND NOT MEASURED, and it is labelled so rather than omitted: WSL2 runs the HOST's architecture, so an arm64 Windows box runs an arm64 Linux distro and therefore this leg (DOCUMENTED, Microsoft's WSL2-on-ARM64 support; no arm64 Windows machine exists in this project to measure it on). Omitting it would have been the worse error — it would say `wsl.exe only works for x86_64`, which is a claim about the launcher that is FALSE, and a Windows/arm64 host would then record `skipped-by-runOn` for the one Linux target it can actually execute.

legs.label: pe64-x86_64
legs.$launchersComment: Wine is the declared cross-OS launcher. It is a DECLARATION, not a claim that it is installed: a host without it records `skipped-emulator-missing` (environmental, loud, promotable to a hard failure) rather than vanishing. No launcher is declared for a non-x86_64 host: Wine alone does not emulate the ISA.

build.$recipeTransformComment: The recipe is derived from a POSIX `make -n`, so it carries that build host's configure/zlib feature probes (HAVE_*/Z_HAVE_*/_HAVE_SQLITE_CONFIG_H) — facts about the DERIVING host, never about this target. `windows-selfconfig` drops them and adds SQLITE_OS_WIN=1 so SQLite self-configures its Windows build. Keyed on THIS LEG, which is why the rule moved out of gen-pe64-manifest.py's prose ('this generator is pe-only, so keying the rule on the pe target is inherent here') into a declaration any driver can read.
build.$zconfGuardsComment: THE HEADER HALF OF THE SAME CROSS-COMPILE CATEGORY ERROR the recipeTransform fixes, and until TF-C115 the ONLY leg it was applied for — by a `perl -0777 -pi` flip buried in one driver's staging step, against ONE zinc/ shared by every leg, which is why a non-pe leg had to be REFUSED (`poisoned`) rather than built. The staged zconf.h comes from the deriving POSIX host, where ./configure wrote `#if 1 → #define Z_HAVE_UNISTD_H`; that is a fact about THAT HOST, and on a Windows TARGET <unistd.h> does not exist. Each guard is now DECLARED per leg and one zinc/ is staged per recipeTransform (stage-zinc.py), so every leg parses a zlib header configured for ITS OWN target and no leg is refused. ★ Z_HAVE_STDARG_H stays true: <stdarg.h> is C-standard and exists on pe. ★ MEASURED (TF-C115) on the elf64-x86_64 leg, both gcc and DSS: with these recipe defines the ONLY thing the guard changes is `z_off_t` = off_t vs long — the same 8-byte `long` on LP64 — and SEEK_*/z_off64_t/the gz* symbol names are byte-identical either way. So the flip is BENIGN on LP64; it is NOT benign on the pe target, where the guard's `#include <unistd.h>` simply does not resolve.
build.$stackReserveComment: D-SQLITE-PE64-FULL-TIER-STACK-DEPTH — Windows defaults a process to 1 MiB; e_fkey-63.1.x recurses to SQLITE_MAX_TRIGGER_DEPTH and overflows it (a NATIVE gcc build overflows too). 8 MiB = what Linux hands the process for free.
build.$librariesComment: pe64 --resolve-library reads a DLL's EXPORT table (.edata), so these must be real DLLs, not import .libs. A DLL is just a FILE: DSS reads a PE export table on any host, so a Linux or macOS box that HAS these files can build this leg. The search paths are candidates on every host (see $noHostKeyingComment).

legs.label: macho64-arm64
legs.$launchersComment: EMPTY, and the emptiness is the hardest-won fact in this file: there is NO off-Mac emulator for a Darwin arm64 executable. Unlike pe-under-Wine or aarch64-under-qemu, the only way to observe this artifact RUN is a real Mac — which is exactly why TF-C113 proved it by BUILDING it on a Windows host and shipping the binary to one. So this leg's build is attempted everywhere and its run is a structural skip everywhere but Darwin/arm64. Do not invent a launcher here.

build.$recipeTransformComment: ⚠ `none` IS WRONG HERE, and TF-C117 is the cycle that could finally SEE it. Until this cycle the leg died at Step 6 — no Darwin libtcl on a non-Mac — so nothing downstream was ever exercised. With the libraries acquired it reaches Step 7 and compiles all 189 TUs, and ✔MEASURED it then fails with 8 diagnostics, of which the load-bearing ones are `error[S0001] got pread64`, `got pwrite64` and `error[S0006] got off64_t`. Those are LINUX names. They arrive because the recipe is derived from a POSIX `make -n` on the deriving Linux host and `_HAVE_SQLITE_CONFIG_H` is passed through verbatim, so this Darwin build inherits THAT host's `HAVE_PREAD64` / `HAVE_OFF64_T` configure answers — the exact cross-compile category error the pe64 leg's `windows-selfconfig` exists to fix, one platform over. The remaining diagnostics (`sysctlbyname`, `CTL_HW`, `HW_AVAILCPU`, `HW_NCPU`) are a separate and genuine gap: a Darwin `<sys/sysctl.h>` descriptor DSS does not ship. Both are tracked as D-HARNESS-MACHO-LEG-INHERITS-THE-DERIVING-LINUX-HOSTS-CONFIGURE-PROBES; the value stays `none` until the transform is designed, because guessing one here would stage a header configuration nobody has measured.
build.$librariesComment: ★ THIS LEG ACQUIRES ITS LIBRARIES (D-HARNESS-LIBRARY-ACQUISITION-BUILT-FOR-ONE-LEG-IN-ONE-DRIVER). It used to declare `host-system`, which on any non-Mac means 'hope this box has a Darwin libtcl' — i.e. it never built anywhere but a Mac, in flat contradiction of the harness's own contract that every leg is BUILT everywhere and only RUN is gated. MacPorts publishes unauthenticated-HTTPS binary archives, and the two we need are UNIVERSAL (one download carries both the arm64 and the x86_64 slice, which is why the sibling macho leg names the SAME url + digest and differs only in the slice it takes). ✔MEASURED 2026-08-04: 110/110 required symbols present on BOTH arches — all 102 `Tcl*` the testfixture imports, 0 missing, plus 8/8 zlib — so there is no eager-import hazard [[D-FFI-DESCRIPTOR-EAGER-IMPORT]].

libraries.$acquireComment: `universal: true` is not a formality. ✔MEASURED: handed the UNIVERSAL file, DSS refuses it — `error[F_UnsupportedBinaryFormat] readImports: '<path>' is a Mach-O FAT/universal binary (big-endian fat_header magic 0xCAFEBABE or 0xCAFEBABF). v1 supports single-arch Mach-O only — slice the required arch first (e.g. `lipo -thin arm64 in.dylib -output out.dylib`). Anchor D-FF1-MACHO-FAT.` — and handed the thin arm64 slice OF THE SAME FILE it succeeds with rc=0. So slicing is the contract that anchor states, performed here because the harness is the only layer that knows which arch this leg wants (`readImports(path, reporter)` takes no target). ⚠ THE REFUSAL'S SPELLING CHANGED INSIDE THIS CYCLE, and the first draft of this comment quoted the older one: `guessFormat` read the fat magic little-endian, so a real universal binary could never reach the arm above and fell into the unknown-magic catch-all instead — the anchor's own remediation was unreachable. That detection bug was fixed in the same cycle; the quote above is the post-fix message. ★ Slicing would be right even if DSS read fat files: a leg's build input should be a library FOR THAT LEG'S TARGET, not a container that also holds a foreign architecture, or 'which architecture did this leg resolve against?' has no answer from the input.
libraries.$importNameComment: ★★ THE TRAP, AND WHY THE ANSWER IS `@loader_path` AND NOT A SYSTEM PATH. Both archives' LC_ID_DYLIB reads `/opt/local/lib/…` (✔MEASURED: `/opt/local/lib/libtcl8.6.dylib`, `/opt/local/lib/libz.1.dylib`), and DSS records a resolved library's EMBEDDED identity as the LC_LOAD_DYLIB — so linking naively produces a Mach-O that demands MacPorts at that prefix on the target Mac. That is a dyld LOAD failure, not a build error, so nothing on this host would catch it. The obvious fix is to record the system path instead — and this project cannot HONESTLY do that for Tcl: nobody here has measured what a Mac carries at /usr/lib for Tcl 8.6, and this repo's own darwin path installs Tcl through Homebrew, whose current `tcl-tk` is 9.x — so `/usr/lib/libtcl8.6.dylib` would be an unverified claim about someone else's machine, and a wrong one costs a dyld failure. `@loader_path/<name>` is TRUE BY CONSTRUCTION: dyld resolves it against the directory holding the executable, the driver stages the acquired dylib there beside the artefact, and the result assumes NOTHING about the target Mac's prefix layout or Tcl version. ⚠ For zlib a system path WOULD be defensible — this harness has measured that `/usr/lib/libz.1.dylib` resolves out of the dyld shared cache even though it cannot be opened as a file (see build-and-test.sh's darwin branch) — but mixing the two policies inside one artefact buys nothing and makes the rule harder to state. Flipping either back to a system path is a one-line edit HERE, which is the point of declaring it.

archives.$memberComment: The archive ships `libz.1.dylib` as a SYMLINK to `libz.1.3.2.dylib`. The declaration names the link, and the resolver follows it inside the archive and materialises the TARGET's bytes under the `as` name — a symlink is not creatable on Windows without privilege and is not a library DSS can read, so one declaration has to work on every host.

legs.label: macho64-x86_64
legs.$launchersComment: Rosetta 2 runs an x86_64 Mach-O on Apple Silicon TRANSPARENTLY, i.e. with no launcher command — but this harness will not model that as 'native', because it is not: it depends on a translation layer that may be absent. `arch -x86_64` is the declared, observable launcher; `arch` is present on every Mac, so a Rosetta-less machine fails at RUN time with a real error instead of a silent pass.

build.$librariesComment: The SAME two MacPorts archives as macho64-arm64 — same url, same pinned digest — because they are UNIVERSAL. What differs is only which slice this leg takes, and that is DERIVED from the leg's own target arch rather than spelled here (see harness_legs.py MACHO_CPU_TYPES). The download is content-addressed by its digest, so the two legs share one fetch and the second is a cache hit with no network at all.

libraries.$importNameComment: See macho64-arm64's $importNameComment — same trap, same answer, and deliberately the same policy on both macho legs so the artefact's dependency shape does not depend on which architecture it was built for.
